articles.title: Make your mobile app findable by AI search
articles.description: If you ship a mobile app, how do AI search tools find it and describe it correctly? They read your website and your store listing, not your app binary. An app with a thin site and a one-line listing gets summarized from whatever scraps exist, and that is how wrong prices and made-up features end up in an answer box. This post covers what a founder who ships a mobile app can fix in an afternoon: the site the app points to, the structured data on it, the store listing, the link between the two, and what the coding agent in your editor reads once it opens your project. It is the mobile half of a topic that web-app guides cover well, such as the Open SaaS guide. That guide's advice (prerender your marketing pages, add JSON-LD, publish an llms.txt file, set meta and Open Graph tags) applies to a mobile app's website too. It stops at the website. A mobile app has more surfaces than that. Surface one: the website, readable without JavaScript The first step is the same for any product. The page a crawler or an assistant fetches has to contain the real content in its HTML. If your marketing site renders everything on the client, an assistant that does not run a full browser sees an empty shell and fills the gap from other sources. We wrote up the failure and the fix in Your website has two front doors, including the check: run curl on your home page and read what comes back. Do that check on three pages: the home page, the page that describes the app, and the pricing or download page. If a price, a platform list or a feature only appears in the browser after scripts run, it does not exist for a reader that skips scripts. Surface two: structured data that says "mobile app" Meta tags tell a crawler about a page. Structured data tells it what the page is. For a mobile app the useful type is MobileApplication, which Schema.org defines as a software application designed to work well on a mobile device. It sits under SoftwareApplication, so every property of that parent is available. A minimal block for your app's page, inside a script tag of type application/ld+json, looks like this: Two properties do most of the work: operatingSystem says where it runs and applicationCategory says what kind of app it is. Once your app is live, add downloadUrl and set it to the address of your real store listing, so the block points at the binary. Pair it with Organization and WebSite blocks on the home page, and an FAQPage block on a page that answers real questions. Validate before you deploy with Google's Rich Results Test or the Schema.org validator. One honest limit: structured data raises the odds that a crawler reads your facts correctly. It does not guarantee a citation, and we have no measured data that it moves the number of installs. Surface three: the store listing Assistants that answer "best app for X" questions often cite the store page, because it is a page with ratings, a category and a description that you do not control the layout of. Treat the listing text as something a machine will read: Say what the app does in the first sentence of the description. Not a slogan: who it is for and what they do with it. Use the same name, price and platform list as your site. A listing that says free and a site that says paid gives an assistant two answers, and it will pick one. Write the subtitle and short description as plain claims you can defend. If the app does not send push notifications today, do not imply it. Keep one source of truth, a short markdown file in your repo with the name, one-line description, platforms, price and category. Paste from it into the listing, the MobileApplication block and the site. When a fact changes, change it once. Surface four: the link between site and app Search and assistants treat the app and the site as one product more readily if you tie them together. Both platforms have a standard way to prove that a domain belongs to an app. On Android, the system fetches a Digital Asset Links file named assetlinks.json from the /.well-known/ folder of each host in your app's intent filters, as Android's App Links documentation (read 22 Nov 2026) describes. On Android 15 and later the system re-verifies in the background, so a change to that file can take up to seven days to reach every device. On iOS the equivalent is an apple-app-site-association file on the same domain plus an associated-domains entry in the app (Apple documents this; we did not re-read the page for this post). The same link helps a person: a link shared from your site opens the app when it is installed and the site when it is not. Check it on a real device, not in the browser. The adb shell pm get-app-links command in the Android documentation prints a verification state for each domain, and verified is the one you want. Surface five: what the coding agent reads Discoverability has a second reader that founders forget: the coding agent that will edit your app. Claude Code, Cursor and similar tools read project files at the root before they write anything. A CLAUDE.md file holds instructions for Claude Code, .cursorrules holds Cursor's rules, and AGENTS.md is a plain file several other tools read. If those files are missing, the agent guesses your stack and your conventions on every prompt. This is what we ship in our own kits. Per our for-agents page and the kit folders on internal main (commit 8ab782e, read 22 Nov 2026), the Booking Kit, the AI SaaS Kit and the Marketplace Kit each carry CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and .cursorrules at the kit root, plus a folder of task prompts: 20 for the Booking Kit, 26 for the AI SaaS Kit and 21 for the Marketplace Kit. The prompt files are named for the change you will ask for, such as adding time zones or deposits to bookings. The files are written for the agent, not for a reader, and they are the same contract a new engineer would want on day one. There is a separate, site-level layer too. Our website serves an llms.txt index of every page, generated from the same inventory as the sitemap so the two cannot drift, and a markdown copy of most pages under /md/. That is for assistants reading the website. The kit files are for the agent inside your editor. They are different files for different readers, and a mobile app needs both. An afternoon checklist Run curl on your home, app and pricing pages. Fix anything that needs scripts to show a price or a platform. Add a MobileApplication block to the app page, and Organization plus WebSite to the home page. Write the one-source-of-truth facts file. Rewrite the store listing's first sentence from it. Host the Android Digital Asset Links file and the iOS association file, then test the Android result with adb shell pm get-app-links. Add CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md to your repo: stack with versions, one rule per concern, and a list of what is out of scope. Publish an llms.txt at your site root. Keep it short and hand-picked, not a copy of the sitemap, unless you generate it from the same inventory. What we do not know We have not measured whether any of these steps changes how often an assistant recommends an app. The keyword behind this topic was below what OpenSEO could measure on 11 Nov 2026, so search demand is small, and the value today is correctness: when an assistant does describe your app, the facts it reads are yours. The effort is an afternoon, and every step is reversible. If your next app is a booking or scheduling product, you can start from one that already has the agent files and the Supabase, Stripe and slot logic in place. The Booking Kit is an Expo app with a typed API server for checkout and reminders, a database rule that blocks double bookings, and a CLAUDE.md, an AGENTS.md and 20 task prompts for your agent: https://otf-kit.dev/templates/booking-kit. It is $99 one-time with 12 months of updates, and the demo is linked from the page. Sources Open SaaS, "SEO and AI discoverability for your SaaS" (prerendering, JSON-LD types, llms.txt, meta and Open Graph), https://docs.opensaas.sh/blog/2026-05-29-seo-and-ai-discoverability-for-your-saas/, dated 29 May 2026, read 22 Nov 2026. Schema.org, MobileApplication type (definition, parent SoftwareApplication, operatingSystem, applicationCategory, downloadUrl), https://schema.org/MobileApplication, read 22 Nov 2026. Android Developers, "Verify Android App Links" (assetlinks.json path, adb pm get-app-links, re-verification latency), https://developer.android.com/training/app-links/verify-android-applinks, read 22 Nov 2026. llms.txt proposal, https://llmstxt.org/, version 2, last modified 10 Aug 2026, read 22 Nov 2026. OTF, "Your website has two front doors. Your AI agent uses the worse one.", https://otf-kit.dev/blog/make-your-website-agent-readable, dated 7 Jul 2026, read 22 Nov 2026. OTF for-agents page and llms.txt route source (kit agent files, prompt counts, site index), otf-kit/internal main commit 8ab782e, read 22 Nov 2026. OTF Booking Kit page, https://otf-kit.dev/templates/booking-kit, read 22 Nov 2026 ($99 one-time, 12 months of updates, Expo SDK 58, Supabase, Stripe checkout).

articles.title: Auditing OpenAI Codex Desktop: 516-Token Cutoffs, Live 1 MiB Git Diffs, and Unzeroed SQLite
articles.description: Co-authored equally by Denis Vaulin (GitHub · LinkedIn) and Oleksii Mai (GitHub · LinkedIn). Interactive Forensic Report: nehumorist.github.io/codex-local-audit Offline Read-Only MIT Auditor (Node.js & Python): github.com/NeHumorist/codex-local-audit In October 2026, OpenAI Codex Desktop running in high / ultra reasoning mode started dropping reasoning output and hiding reasoning summaries while burning through subscription quota faster. Rather than guess from UI symptoms, we ran a cross-platform forensic audit across: 1,502 local ~/.codex/ session rollouts across Windows 11 x64 (215 sessions / 34,523 calls) and macOS arm64 (1,287 sessions / 160,172 calls), plus an independent third-party Pro reproduction across 246.8k calls; Signed client binaries (OpenAI.Codex_26.1111.2228.0 on Windows x64 and v26.1111.71704 on macOS arm64 — both codex and app.asar) cross-checked against the public openai/codex Rust repository; Local SQLite stores (queue_1.sqlite, logs_2.sqlite, thread_history_1.sqlite, codex-dev.db, memories_1.sqlite) and dictation-history/; Two official EU GDPR "Export Data" archives from OpenAI. Everything below is reproducible offline on your own machine in 5 seconds using our read-only MIT tool. 1. The Quantized 516-Token Cutoff Wall (518k - 2 Harmonics) Across both our Plus/Pro datasets and an independent third-party Pro user's 246.8k-call dataset, reasoning output exhibits a sharp discontinuity at exactly 516 tokens: Dataset Calls at 515 Calls at 516 Calls at 517 1034 (2 blocks) 1552 (3 blocks) 2070 (4 blocks) 3rd-Party Pro (246.8k calls) 70 9,021 0 1,280 384 139 macOS (160.2k calls) — 9,392 1 1,608 497 169 Three checks confirm this is not a tokenizer quirk or a simple rate-limit artifact: Harmonic spacing at 518k - 2: spikes repeat cleanly at 516, 1034, 1552, and 2070 reasoning tokens. Ciphertext byte-length correlation (r = 0.99538): reasoning_output_tokens tracks the raw encrypted_content ciphertext byte lengths directly (rTok == 0 calls carry 0 encrypted reasoning bytes). Not a quota ceiling: 71.2% (and 78.7% on macOS) of exact-516 cutoffs occurred below 80% on both the 5-hour and 7-day subscription windows. Alongside this cutoff, turn_context.summary silently flipped from "detailed" to "none" without a client update. 2. Live 1 MiB Raw git diff Capture Firing While Opted Out Inspecting signed app.asar (907538.0572f09d40.js, verified byte-for-byte across Windows and macOS builds) shows a telemetry payload (codex_turn_diff_event) that captures up to 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) of raw unified git diff source code (diff, between_turn_diff, session_start_diff, visualization_diff, repository_full_name, commit/tree SHAs) and sends it to /wham/analytics-events/events. The gate checks only is_zdr === false and Statsig gate 586515394 — performing zero checks of training_allowed: false or [analytics] enabled = false. In live Windows Desktop runtime logs (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Codex\Logs, 2026-11-05), we captured post-gate execution (method=turn-diff-capture-complete workerId=git -> Failed to complete turn diff analytics capture) tied to the exact EU account whose official OpenAI GDPR export records: 3. Windows Explorer UserAssist Scraping & Default-On Analytics Inside signed app.asar, embedded PowerShell (Get-UserAssistEntries, Decode-Rot13) reads Windows Explorer's HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\UserAssist\*\Count registry keys and writes a catalog of installed third-party applications (last_used, use_count) to ~/.codex/cache/computer-use/computer-use-app-catalog/.../user-assist.json. On our Windows test host, user-assist.json cached 82 non-OpenAI applications (alongside 28 [external-agent-import] scans of competitor directories like ~/.claude and .cursor). At the same time, while OpenAI's Rust CLI source (cli/src/main.rs) comments that analytics default to off for app-server, Electron unconditionally passes --analytics-default-enabled, and Codex Settings provides 0 UI toggles to disable telemetry. 4. Local SQLite Erasure Gaps, Microphone Retention & Incomplete GDPR Exports 0 calls to PRAGMA secure_delete across all 10,502 files of openai/codex and signed binaries: queue_1.sqlite measured 98.6% unzeroed freelist pages at 0 live rows (+ recoverable prompts in -wal), and logs_2.sqlite measured 90.6%–91.8% unzeroed deleted pages. thread_history_1.sqlite contains 0 ON DELETE CASCADE foreign keys and is skipped by StateRuntime::delete_thread. dictation-history/ retains unencrypted local Opus microphone audio + transcripts with zero TTL (54+ days on Windows; up to 78 days including cancelled captures on macOS). Plaintext auth.json on Windows: codex_desktop_secret_auth_storage explicitly excludes Windows. 0 of 1,502 Codex sessions appeared across two official EU GDPR "Export Data" archives (150.8 MB and 186.8 MB), even though export_manifest.json reported "omissions": []. 5. Negative Controls: What We Checked and Ruled Out To keep every claim anchored strictly to verifiable bytes, our report explicitly documents 10 hypotheses we checked and ruled out, including: CodexWindowsSystemSerialObserved (gate 1259783540): unhashed Windows BIOS serial collection and local debug-log redaction are compiled into signed app.asar, but the gate had not activated on our test host. 0 local model_reroute events inside ~/.codex/sessions/ JSONL records. Standard 5h/7d quota exhaustion (ruled out because >71% of 516 cutoffs occurred below 80% quota). Verify Your Own Machine in 5 Seconds (MIT, Read-Only, Offline) codex-local-audit has full feature parity across zero-dependency Node.js (22.15+ / 24+) and Python 3.10+. It opens every SQLite database strictly read-only, makes zero network calls, never opens or reads auth.json, and strips all prompts, code, app names, and file paths. git clone https://github.com/NeHumorist/codex-local-audit.git cd codex-local-audit # Node.js 22.15+ / 24+ (zero external dependencies) node audit_codex.mjs # Or Python 3.10–3.13 via uv uv run --with zstandard python audit_codex.py On Windows without a global Node 24 install, you can invoke the Node 24 runtime already bundled with Codex Desktop: $node24 = Get-ChildItem "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\*\bin\node.exe" | Select-Object -First 1 -ExpandProperty FullName & $node24 .\audit_codex.mjs Interactive Forensic Report: https://nehumorist.github.io/codex-local-audit/ Source Code (MIT): https://github.com/NeHumorist/codex-local-audit If you run the audit on Codex Plus or Pro, feel free to share anonymized counts in the comments — we are especially interested in whether the 516 / 1034 / 1552 pattern reproduces on newer builds.

I built an AI deal bot on a Mac mini — but a human approves every post
articles.description: Why I built it I'm an IT director by day in Raleigh, NC. I love a good deal, but I hate deal sites. Most of them post everything: 70%-off off-brand gadgets, "deals" on laptops with 8 GB of RAM, sales that ended three hours ago. You scroll past 50 bad items to find one good one. So I built Snag Bag Deals (snagbagdeals.com): a small deal site where software does the scanning and a person does the deciding. A Python bot on a Mac mini in my house reads deal feeds all day, an AI model throws out the junk, and every survivor lands on my phone as a card I approve or skip. Nothing goes public without a tap from me. It's been live about a week. In that time the bot has looked at more than 16,000 items, sent me about 1,150 approval cards, and I've posted 278 deals. Here's how it works, what it costs, and what went wrong. How it works The pipeline has four steps, and only the last one is me. Deal feeds. The bot polls 13 RSS feeds and deal pages (Slickdeals, DealNews, 9to5Toys, camelcamelcamel and others) every few minutes and pulls out the store link. Keyword rules. Cheap checks run first, before any AI call: a blocklist, duplicates, stores I don't support, and "save up to X%" sale pages that aren't one product. AI filter. Whatever survives goes to Claude's smallest model with my written guidelines ("good items people will get use out of, not something they regret"). It answers keep or skip, picks a category, cleans up the title and writes a one-line blurb. My recent taps are included as examples, so it learns my taste. My approval. Keepers arrive in Telegram as a card with the price, the source and Post / Skip / Never buttons. One tap publishes to the static site (rebuilt and deployed to Cloudflare Pages within a minute), a Telegram channel, and an email roundup twice a week. Facebook and Threads only get the few best deals each day, spread out, so the feeds don't read like spam. Keeping deals honest after they post A deal is only good while the price holds, and Amazon prices move hourly. Without access to Amazon's product API (it unlocks after 10 sales in 30 days), the bot can't read live prices, and scraping Amazon is against the affiliate rules. So it leans on a few cheaper signals: Source checks. It re-opens each deal's original post and looks for "expired" or "sold out" in the title. Slickdeals and friends mark dead deals quickly. Flash deals expire on a timer. Lightning deals and today-only deals are marked dead when their window closes, no check needed. A morning check, riskiest first. Each morning I get up to 10 deals to eyeball, ranked by how likely they are to be wrong: promo-code deals, Lightning deals, anything over 60% off. One tap marks a dead one. Visitor reports. Every card has an "Expired? Report it" button. Fix once, fix everywhere. One command corrects a price on the site, the Telegram post, the live Facebook post and any social posts still in the queue. Expired deals get edited to say so on each platform that allows edits. The site also stops showing a price once a deal is a day old and labels it "check price," which is more honest than a stale number. What it costs to run The whole thing runs for about the price of the domain. The AI filter is the only metered cost, and it's small because it uses a fast, cheap model on short prompts. Piece What runs it Cost The bot Python on a Mac mini I already own (also my Plex server) $0 AI filtering and blurbs Claude's smallest model via API about 14 cents a day Website + hosting Static pages on Cloudflare Pages Analytics A Cloudflare Pages Function writing to Analytics Engine Email roundup Kit, free plan Domain Cloudflare Registrar about $11 a year The bot is light enough to share a home server: about 50 MB of memory and a couple percent of one CPU core on average. It logs its own costs too. Every API charge, receipt and payout lands in a small money log, which feeds a private stats page and a CSV for taxes. Analytics are first-party and cookie-free. The page sends a tiny beacon to my own endpoint with the page, the source and whether it was a click out. No IP addresses are stored, no profiles, no Google Analytics. What went wrong (so far) The bot read a store credit as the price. A headset deal mentioned a gift-card bonus, and the parser took that dollar amount as the sale price. Now amounts next to words like "credit," "gift card" and "rebate" are ignored. "eCoupon at checkout" slipped past it. A $47 meat thermometer posted at $14.99 because the deal needed a one-time promo code the bot didn't recognize. It catches that wording now, and promo-code deals get flagged for a check the next morning. "Clip the coupon" was too broad. Some deals need a coupon you tick on the page; others apply a discount at checkout. Calling both "clip the coupon" sent people looking for a box that wasn't there, so they're two different labels now. Posting fast from a new account looks like spam. Bluesky flagged the account after a burst of link posts on day one. Now social accounts get only the few best deals a day, spaced out. The site and Telegram still get everything. Affiliate networks want traffic first. Two networks turned the site down this week, politely, for being too new. Amazon's product API also waits until you have sales. The fix is boring: keep posting good deals and grow. What's next The building part went fast. I wrote it with Claude as a pair programmer, and the first working version took about a week of evenings. The hard part now is the one AI doesn't do for you: getting people to show up and trust it. Next up is a reader request form that already exists but needs readers: tell me what you're shopping for, a daily job hunts for it, and matches get a Reader request tag. After that, product photos once Amazon's API opens up. I'd love feedback, especially on two things: Would you use a curated deal site like this, or are deals strictly a "go to Slickdeals" thing for you? If you've grown a small content site from zero, what channel actually worked: email, Telegram, search, something else? The site is snagbagdeals.com. Happy to answer questions about the bot in the comments. Disclosure: Snag Bag Deals earns a commission from Amazon and other stores on qualifying purchases, at no extra cost to you.
